analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $11 an hour and indexes it to inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have raised the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $11 over two years, was never considered by the committee it was assigned to and died when Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise the federal minimum wage in three steps — to $8.50, then $10.00, then $11.00 an hour — and after three years adjust it every year automatically with the cost of living. It would also raise the cash wage employers must pay tipped workers, such as restaurant servers, from $2.13 an hour toward 70% of the full minimum. The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and no vote was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly two million-plus workers who earn the federal minimum wage or close to it, plus tipped workers like restaurant servers, whose cash pay would rise from $2.13 an hour toward 70% of the full minimum. Communities where low-wage workers would spend their extra pay would also see more consumer spending.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage in three steps to $8.50, then $10.00, then $11.00 an hour over two years [S3].

After three years, requires the Secretary of Labor to raise the wage every year by the increase in the Consumer Price Index, so it no longer loses value to inflation between congressional updates [S3].
Raises the cash wage for tipped employees to $3.00 an hour in year one, then increases it annually until it equals 70% of the full minimum wage [S3].
Requires the Department of Labor to publish each scheduled increase 60 days in advance in the Federal Register and on its website, giving employers notice [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay the federal minimum wage, especially restaurant chains and other food service and retail employers, who would face higher labor costs; some of that cost would be passed to consumers through prices, and the bill's gradual schedule and advance-notice requirement are designed to soften the transition.

drawbacks.text: Raises labor costs for employers that pay the minimum wage, particularly restaurants that currently pay tipped workers a cash wage of as little as $2.13 an hour, which the bill would push up to 70% of the full minimum [S3].

Supporters of the existing lower tipped wage argue that a larger cash wage plus indexing would squeeze small restaurants' margins and could lead to higher prices or fewer tipped jobs; the bill's phased schedule partially but not fully addresses this [S3].
Once indexing begins, the wage would rise automatically each year with inflation, removing Congress's regular opportunity to review the level in light of economic conditions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the gains are direct and substantial: a phased raise to $11 an hour, a higher cash wage for tipped workers, and automatic inflation adjustments. The costs fall on specific employers — especially restaurants and other low-wage industries — as higher payroll costs, likely passed partly to consumers as higher prices. This is a standard transfer from low-wage employers and their customers to low-wage workers; the main honest uncertainty is the size of any employment effect, which economists debate. The bill's two-year phase-in and advance notice limit disruption.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Representative John Larson introduced the bill on December 12, 2013, in the first session of the 113th Congress [S1].
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day [S5].
No member of the House signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The committee took no further action, and the bill never received a vote in the House or Senate before the Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that pay the federal minimum wage — particularly restaurant and food service employers — are better off, because the federal minimum wage remained at $7.25 and the tipped cash wage at $2.13 an hour.

for.name: Rep. John B. Larson
for.role: U.S. Representative from Connecticut and sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to committee; no other member cosponsored it.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the federal minimum wage
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a markup, hearing, or vote on it.

against.name: Rep. John Kline
against.role: Chair of the House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: As chair, controlled the committee's agenda and never scheduled action on the bill.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Did not bring a minimum wage increase to the House floor during the 113th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Democrat with no cosponsors, and a Republican-controlled committee and House majority took no action on any version of a federal minimum wage increase during the session.

industries.note: The bill would raise the required cash wage for tipped workers from $2.13 an hour toward 70% of the full minimum, ending the widest use of the federal tip credit, and raise the base wage floor that applies to fast-food and other food service workers. Restaurants' interest in keeping wages at $2.13 runs directly against the workers the bill serves.
Employers paying the $7.25 federal minimum would face payroll costs up to $11 an hour over two years. Their savings from the bill dying is the mirror of the wage loss to low-wage workers.
Not an industry but the main affected group: about a step raise to $11 an hour plus automatic inflation adjustments, with tipped workers gaining the largest relative increase.
